Sequential dependencies
text:
Contraction vs expansion
The above analyses do not tell us whether participants adapt their for the next trial depending on whether it currently contained the target or not. To see this, we want to measure the proportion of expanding vs contracting arcs conditional on whether the previous trial was a hit or not. For a single metric, we can calculate the likelihood ratio of expanding vs contracting conditional on hit or not
\[
\frac{Pr(a_{n+1} > a_n \,|\, a_n \geq abs(y_n))}{Pr(a_{n+1} \leq a_n \,|\, a_n \geq abs(y_n))}
\]

smry1 <- exp1 |> 
  group_by(subject, experimentorder) |> 
  calculate_expand_likelihood_ratio()

smry1 |> 
  plot_likelihood_ratio()







Each point is a single subject, and each subject has as point for hits and a point after misses. First, we see that the likelihood ratio is much more variable after a miss. This is partly due to the low level of misses overall. We see a tendency for contraction after hits (likelihood ratio < 1) and tendency for expansion after misses (likelihood ratio > 1). This is supported by one sample t-tests:

t.test(filter(smry1, resp_type == "hit")$likelihood_ratio_expand, mu = 1, alternative = "less")

The experiment uses an interleaved design where the set size varies on each trial. Since arc responses vary strongly with set-size, what we are interested in is how their response changes not only from the previous trial but from what it would have been given the set size that they see. We can check if we compare the change direction with the previous time they encountered the same set size, depending on that previous time was a hit or miss. There can be any number of intervening trials and we only care about the last time that the same setsize occurred. We get a similar dependency:

The graph and stats look like before but they tell us something different - people remember what arc they gave the previous time they encountered a given setsize and whether they hit or missed. When they encounter the same setsize condition, they tend to expand their arc relative to the one they gave to the previous trial of the same set size, not just the immediately previous trial, specifically if they missed last time with that set size.
So from the two analyses combined we know that people adapt their arc (expand or contract) based on at least two sources of information - the immediately preceding trial, and the last trial that had the same setsize condition.

section: Simulated adaptive algorithm and compare to bootstrap
text:
Simulated adaptive algorithm and compare to bootstrap
Maybe my intuition is incorrect, and this is what we expect with the adaptation algorithm? Let’s see the expected data for a simulated agent using our algorithm 4 / 5. We will compare their expansion likelihood ratio when using the adaptation vs shuffled bootstrap.

sim_algo4 <- algo4(delta = 0.01) |> run_arc_algorithm(n_trials = 1000, init_arc = 1)
sim_algo4 <- data.frame(resperr = sim_algo4$y, arc = sim_algo4$a * 2)
sim_algo5 <- algo5() |> run_arc_algorithm(n_trials = 1000)
sim_algo5 <- data.frame(resperr = sim_algo5$y, arc = sim_algo5$a * 2)

Under algorithm 4 by design the agent never expands after a hit and never contracts after a miss.

sim_algo4 |> 
  calculate_expand_likelihood_ratio()

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  resp_type contracting expanding likelihood_ratio_expand
  <chr>           <dbl>     <dbl>                   <dbl>
1 hit                 1         0                       0
2 miss                0         1                     Inf


Algorithm 5 occasionally expands after a hit and contracts after a miss but very rarely and much less than in the human data.

sim_algo5 |> 
  calculate_expand_likelihood_ratio()

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  resp_type contracting expanding likelihood_ratio_expand
  <chr>           <dbl>     <dbl>                   <dbl>
1 hit             0.941    0.0586                  0.0622
2 miss            0.482    0.518                   1.08  



out <- replicate(1000, bootstrap_lr_shuffled_arcs(sim_algo5), simplify = FALSE)
out <- do.call(rbind, out)

Here is the result. The figure shows the expected likelihood ratio for expanding the arc for the simulated data from algorithm 5 when shuffling the arcs.

out |> 
  mutate(likelihood_ratio_expand = mean_ratio) |> 
  plot_likelihood_ratio()







The regression to the mean effect is real here too, and of the same magnitude, but it accounts for a very minor proportion of contractions after hits. After misses the algorithm LLR for expansion is 1.10185, which is smaller than 68% of the shuffled LLRs.
Normally this would indicate that the expansion isn’t due to adaptation but due to regression to the mean. However, in this case we know the ground truth - the algorithm does expand after misses! See section Visualizing algorithm 5 of the reinforcement learning notebook. It only does that after narrow misses, so that’s why the likelihood ratio for expansion is small. In this case, even though the effect size is consistent with what is expected under regression to the mean, we know there is no regression to the mean because the arc size is determined deterministically.
This finding means that shuffling the arcs is not necessarily a good control, and depends on the assumptions we put in (that the arc is a random sample from a distribution).

title: Optimal arc to maximize reward
text:
Participants received points based on how wide their arc was and whether it included the target. The formula for the points \(p\) is:
\[
p = \left(\pi - \alpha\right)\bigl[|y| \le \alpha \bigr].
\]
where \(y\) is the distance between the point response and the target, and the square brackets are Iverson bracket notation that evaluates to 1 if the statement is true and 0 otherwise. \(\alpha\) is the half-width of the symmetric arc around the response. All variables are in radians (although the points received were based on degrees).
The equation for \(p\) suggests that given a fixed distribution for the random variable \(Y\), there might be an optimal arc width response. When you decrease the arc width you get more points due to the \(\pi-\alpha\) term, but you increase the probability that you miss the target and receive 0 points.
We can analytically determine what the optimal \(\alpha\) would be for any given distribution on \(Y\). We want to maximize the expected reward. Let \(g: \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^+\) be a function of \(\alpha\) that gives the expected reward:
\[
g(\alpha) = \mathbb{E}[p] = \left(\pi - \alpha\right)\text{Pr}(|Y| \leq \alpha), \quad 0\leq \alpha \leq \pi.
\]
Let \(F(y)\) be the cumulative distribution function for \(Y\). Then the probability that the absolute value of Y is less than or equal to \(\alpha\) is:
\[
\text{Pr}(|Y| \leq \alpha) = F(\alpha) - F(-\alpha).
\]
If we assume a symmetric unimodal distribution around 0, \(F(-\alpha) = 1 - F(\alpha)\) and so our expression for \(g(\alpha)\) simplifies to:
\[
g(\alpha) = \left(\pi - \alpha \right) \left(2F(\alpha) - 1\right).
\]
To maximize the expected reward, we can find where the first derivative of \(g\) vanishes. Differentiate and set equal to 0:
\[
\begin{aligned}
g'(\alpha) = -(2F(\alpha)-1) + \left(\pi - \alpha \right)2F'(\alpha) = 0 \\
\left(\pi - \alpha \right) F'(\alpha) = F(\alpha) - 0.5
\end{aligned}
\]
The optimal \(\alpha\) is the value the solution to that equation. It can also be expressed as a fixed point form for the optimal value for \(\alpha\):
\[
\alpha = \pi - \frac{F(\alpha) - 0.5}{F'(\alpha)} = \pi - \frac{F(\alpha) - 0.5}{f(\alpha)}
\]
where \(f(\alpha)\) is the probability density.

title: Optimal arc to maximize reward
text:
Theoretical changes in optimal responses
The above analysis tells us that given a specific memory distribution, there is a theoretically optimal arc width, which also corresponds to a theoretically optimal hit rate - the proportion of trials on which the the arc includes the target. We can use these equations to find how the optimum arc width and hit rate changes as some parameter of the distribution changes.
The simplest case and a sanity check is the optimum under a uniform distribution on \((-\pi,\pi]\) with no information.
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(y) &= \frac{1}{2\pi}, \quad F(y) = \frac{\pi+y}{2\pi} \\
\alpha &= \pi - \frac{\frac{\pi+\alpha}{2\pi}-0.5}{\frac{1}{2\pi}} = \pi - \alpha \\
\alpha &= \pi/2
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(\alpha\) is the half-width arc in radians, it means that the optimal full arc under no information is exactly half the circle.
Now, let’s take the SDM and vary the \(c\) parameter and find the optimum arc width and hit rate. Here are the results for one set of parameters (note that alpha is the half-width arc in radians).

library(bmm)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)

source("R/arc-models.R")

find_optimum_sdm(c = 4, kappa = 4)

      alpha      phit
1 0.6787451 0.7483018


So let’s vary \(c\), with fixed \(\kappa = 3\):

cs <- seq(0, 10, 0.01)
sdm_optim <- lapply(cs, \(c) find_optimum_sdm(c, kappa = 3))
sdm_optim <- do.call(rbind, sdm_optim)
sdm_optim$c <- cs
sdm_optim_long <- gather(sdm_optim, variable, optimal_value, alpha, phit)


sdm_optim_long |> 
  ggplot(aes(c, optimal_value)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free")







As the strength of the memory distribution increases, the optimal arc width decreases, and the optimal hit rate increases as well. This was the first surprise to me - it was clear that the optimal arc will become smaller, but I had thought that the optimal hit rate might be a constant level!
This means we can test whether people’s actual arc responses and hit rates conform to optimality under perfect information about the shape of their memory distribution.

Because we have full posterior samples for the sdm parameters, we can determine a posterior prediction for the optimal arc size and hit probability given the parameters of each posterior sample. First, do this using only the population parameters for setsize, similar to the pooled empirical predictions above.

extract_var_draws <- function(draws, var) {
  vars <- paste0("b_", var, "_setsize", 1:8)
  draws <- draws[,vars]
  names(draws) <- 1:8
  exp(draws)
}

h_draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(fit)
c_draws <- extract_var_draws(h_draws, "c")
kappa_draws <- extract_var_draws(h_draws, "kappa")


# reshape
c_draws_long <- gather(c_draws, setsize, c)
kappa_draws_long <- gather(kappa_draws, setsize, kappa)
population_posterior <- cbind(c_draws_long, kappa_draws_long[,"kappa"])

# extract the optimums
population_optimum_posterior <- purrr::pmap(population_posterior, \(setsize, c, kappa) find_optimum_sdm(c, kappa))
population_optimum_posterior <- do.call(rbind, population_optimum_posterior)
population_optimum_posterior$setsize <- population_posterior$setsize

# plot the optimums
observed_arc_phit_long <- observed_arc_phit |> 
  rename(arc = arc_obs, phit = phit_obs) |> 
  gather(measure, value, -setsize)
population_optimum_posterior |> 
  rename(arc = alpha) |> 
  gather(measure, value, -setsize) |> 
  ggplot(aes(setsize, value)) + 
  geom_violin() +
  geom_point(data = observed_arc_phit_long, color = "red") +
  geom_line(data = observed_arc_phit_long, color = "red", aes(group = 1)) +
  facet_wrap(~measure)







The red dots and line are the observed median arc width and hit rate. The white violin plots show the posterior distributions for predicted optimal arc width and hit rates from the SDM, using the population parameter estimates.
Since this was a hierarchical model, we can estimate predicted optimal behavior for each subject and setsize condition. We can get a full posterior for the optimality coefficient.

extract_var_draws_subj <- function(draws, var, subject_ids) {
  pop_vars <- paste0("b_", var, "_setsize", 1:8)
  pop_draws <- as.data.frame(draws[,pop_vars])
  subj_draws <- posterior::extract_variable_array(
    draws, 
    variable = paste0("r_subject__", var), 
    with_chains = FALSE
  )
  
  for (s in seq_len(length(pop_vars))) {
    subj_draws[,,s] <- subj_draws[,,s] + pop_draws[,s]
  }
  subj_draws <- subj_draws[,subject_ids,]
  dimnames(subj_draws)[[2]] <- subject_ids
  dimnames(subj_draws)[[3]] <- 1:8
  exp(subj_draws)
}

subjects <- as.numeric(as.character(sort(unique(ss_exp$subject))))
c_draws <- extract_var_draws_subj(h_draws, "c", subjects)
kappa_draws <- extract_var_draws_subj(h_draws, "kappa", subjects)


# reshape
c_draws_long <- as.data.frame.table(c_draws, responseName = "value")
colnames(c_draws_long) <- c("iteration", "subject", "setsize", "c")
kappa_draws_long <- as.data.frame.table(kappa_draws, responseName = "value")
colnames(kappa_draws_long) <- c("iteration", "subject", "setsize", "kappa")
subj_posterior <- left_join(c_draws_long, kappa_draws_long)

# extract the optimums. Takes a long time
file <- "output/subj_optimum_posterior.rds"
if (fs::file_exists(file)) {
  subj_optimum_posterior <- readRDS(file)
} else {
  subj_optimum_posterior <- purrr::pmap(subj_posterior[,c("c","kappa")], find_optimum_sdm)
  subj_optimum_posterior <- do.call(rbind, subj_optimum_posterior)
  subj_optimum_posterior <- cbind(subj_optimum_posterior, subj_posterior[,c("subject", "setsize")])
  saveRDS(subj_optimum_posterior, file)
}



# plot the optimums
observed_arc_phit_subj <- ss_exp |> 
  group_by(subject, setsize) |> 
  summarise(arc = median(arc/2),
            phit = mean(hit))
observed_arc_phit_subj_long <- observed_arc_phit_subj |> 
  gather(measure, value, -setsize, -subject)


points_by_setsize_subject <- ss_exp |> 
  group_by(setsize, subject) |> 
  summarise(points_obs = mean(points)) |> 
  mutate(subject = as.factor(subject))

subj_optimum_posterior <- subj_optimum_posterior |> 
  mutate(points_pred = rad2deg(pi - alpha)*phit) |>

title: Model diagnostics: noisy-gradient (algo5), MLE
text:
library(tidyverse)
library(bmm)
source("R/arc-models.R")
source("R/utils.R")
source("R/math.R")

title: Model diagnostics: noisy-gradient (algo5), MLE
text:
Task and model summary
On each trial a participant reports a remembered color (continuous response) and sets a symmetric arc of half-width \(a_t \in (0,\pi)\) around it. Points are awarded as \[
p_t = (\pi - a_t)\,\mathbf{1}\!\bigl[|y_t| \le a_t\bigr],
\] where \(y_t\) is the signed response error. Wider arcs are safer but earn fewer points, creating an accuracy–confidence tradeoff. Empirically, participants’ arc widths are near-optimal given their error distributions.
Response errors are modelled by the Signal Discrimination Model (SDM): \[
y_t \sim \text{SDM}(c,\kappa).
\]
Arc-width updates follow a noisy stochastic-gradient rule on the logit-reparameterized arc \(x_t = \operatorname{logit}(a_t/\pi)\). We do this on the unconstrained \(x_t\) so that despite adding random noise, responses that get mapped back to \(a_{t+1} = \operatorname{invlogit}(x_{t+1})\pi\) are in the right range, \((0,\pi)\), without needing to truncate. Define a soft hit indicator and gradient: \[
s_t = \sigma\!\left(\frac{a_t - |y_t|}{\tau}\right), \qquad
g_t = -s_t + (\pi - a_t)\,\frac{s_t(1-s_t)}{\tau},
\] with a decaying learning rate \(\delta_t = \delta_0/(t+1)^{0.5}\). The state transition is \[
x_{t+1} = x_t + \delta_t\bigl(g_t + \varepsilon_t\bigr), \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_g^2).
\]
Joint log-likelihood. Because \(x_{t+1} \mid x_t, y_t\) is normal, the full log-likelihood decomposes as \[
\ell(\theta) =
\underbrace{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log f_{\text{SDM}}(y_t \mid c,\kappa)}_{\text{response errors}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\log\phi\!\left(x_{t+1};\; x_t + \delta_t\, g_t,\; \delta_t\,\sigma_g\right)}_{\text{arc transitions}},
\] with fitted parameter vector \(\theta=(c,\kappa,\tau,\delta_0,\sigma_g)\). The exponent \(\delta_{\text{pow}}=0.5\) is fixed. Below we verify identifiability via simulation-based parameter recovery and maximum-likelihood estimation with optim.

title: Model diagnostics: noisy-gradient (algo5), MLE
text:
Simulate data
Generate a single subject’s worth of data from the noisy-gradient model with known parameters. We use run_arc_algorithm which feeds SDM-generated response errors y through the update function trial by trial.

true_pars <- list(c = 6, kappa = 3, tau = 0.025, delta0 = 0.1, sigma_g = 2)

set.seed(4233)
sim <- run_arc_algorithm(
  arc_update_fun = algo5_noisy_grad(
    tau = true_pars$tau,
    delta0 = true_pars$delta0,
    delta_pow = 0.5,
    sigma_g = true_pars$sigma_g
  ),
  c = true_pars$c,
  kappa = true_pars$kappa,
  init_arc = pi/8,
  n_trials = 1000
)

par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(sim$a, type = "l", xlab = "Trial", ylab = "Arc width")
hist(sim$a, xlab = "Arc width")
hist(sim$y, xlab = "Response error")






par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

title: Model diagnostics: noisy-gradient (algo5), MLE
text:
Log-likelihood
The joint log-likelihood has two additive components:


SDM component — the density of each response error \(y_t\)


Arc-transition component — a normal density on the logit scale for the arc update from trial \(t\) to \(t+1\)


The functions algo5_loglik, par_to_unconstrained, par_from_unconstrained, and neg_loglik are defined in R/arc-models.R (loaded above). All five parameters are strictly positive, so we estimate on the log scale and exponentiate back.

title: Model diagnostics: noisy-gradient (algo5), MLE
text:
Fit with optim

We initialise at perturbed values (not the truth) to verify that the optimiser can recover the generating parameters.

init_pars <- list(c = 3, kappa = 5, tau = 0.05, delta0 = 0.05, sigma_g = 1)
theta0 <- par_to_unconstrained(init_pars)

fit <- optim(
  par = theta0,
  fn = neg_loglik,
  y = sim$y,
  a = sim$a,
  method = "Nelder-Mead",
  control = list(maxit = 5000, reltol = 1e-10)
)

fit$convergence  # 0 = success

[1] 0

text:
Compare estimated vs true parameters

estimated <- par_from_unconstrained(fit$par)

comparison <- tibble(
  parameter = names(true_pars),
  initial = unlist(init_pars),
  true_value = unlist(true_pars),
  estimated = unlist(estimated)
)

title: Model diagnostics: noisy-gradient (algo5), MLE
text:
Likelihood profile at the MLE
A quick sanity check: evaluate the likelihood over a grid around each MLE estimate while holding the others fixed, to confirm we are at a peak.

best_theta <- fit$par
par_names <- c("c", "kappa", "tau", "delta0", "sigma_g")

profiles <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_along(par_names), \(j) {
  grid <- seq(best_theta[j] - 1, best_theta[j] + 1, length.out = 80)
  ll_vals <- sapply(grid, \(v) {
    theta_tmp <- best_theta
    theta_tmp[j] <- v
    -neg_loglik(theta_tmp, y = sim$y, a = sim$a)
  })
  tibble(
    parameter = par_names[j],
    theta_unconstrained = grid,
    value = exp(grid),
    loglik = ll_vals
  )
})

ggplot(profiles, aes(x = value, y = loglik)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(data = comparison, aes(xintercept = estimated), linetype = "dashed", color = "blue") +
  geom_vline(data = comparison, aes(xintercept = true_value), linetype = "dotted", color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~parameter, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Parameter value", y = "Log-likelihood",
       caption = "Blue dashed = MLE, Red dotted = true value")

title: Model diagnostics: noisy-gradient (algo5), MLE
text:
Parameter recovery
Sample 10000 parameter sets uniformly, simulate data for each, fit via MLE, and check whether the true values are recovered.

n_recovery <- 10000
n_trials <- 1000
set.seed(2026)

recovery_true <- tibble(
  iter = seq_len(n_recovery),
  c = runif(n_recovery, 1, 10),
  kappa = runif(n_recovery, 1, 10),
  tau = runif(n_recovery, 0.001, 0.05),
  delta0 = runif(n_recovery, 0.01, 0.2),
  sigma_g = runif(n_recovery, 0, 10)
)

fit_one <- function(iter, c, kappa, tau, delta0, sigma_g) {
  sim <- run_arc_algorithm(
    arc_update_fun = algo5_noisy_grad(tau = tau, delta0 = delta0,
                                       delta_pow = 0.5, sigma_g = sigma_g),
    c = c, kappa = kappa, init_arc = pi / 2, n_trials = n_trials
  )

  theta0 <- par_to_unconstrained(list(
    c = 4, kappa = 4, tau = 0.02, delta0 = 0.08, sigma_g = 3
  ))

  fit <- tryCatch(
    optim(par = theta0, fn = neg_loglik, y = sim$y, a = sim$a,
          method = "Nelder-Mead",
          control = list(maxit = 5000, reltol = 1e-10)),
    error = \(e) list(par = rep(NA_real_, 5), convergence = 99)
  )

  est <- par_from_unconstrained(fit$par)
  tibble(
    iter = iter,
    c_est = est$c, kappa_est = est$kappa, tau_est = est$tau,
    delta0_est = est$delta0, sigma_g_est = est$sigma_g,
    converged = fit$convergence == 0
  )
}

recovery_est <- with_cache("output/algo5_recovery_est.rds", {
  purrr::pmap_dfr(recovery_true, fit_one)
})

Tag iterations where at least one estimate exceeds 4× the max true generating value:

est_cols <- c("c_est", "kappa_est", "tau_est", "delta0_est", "sigma_g_est")

thresholds <- 4 * sapply(true_cols, \(col) max(recovery_true[[col]]))

})

title: Model diagnostics: contraction-expansion (algo4) with logit noise, MLE
text:
Task and model summary
On each trial a participant reports a remembered color (continuous response) and sets a symmetric arc of half-width \(a_t \in (0,\pi)\) around it. Points are awarded as \[
p_t = (\pi - a_t)\,\mathbf{1}\!\bigl[|y_t| \le a_t\bigr],
\] where \(y_t\) is the signed response error. Wider arcs are safer but earn fewer points, creating an accuracy–confidence tradeoff. Empirically, participants’ arc widths are near-optimal given their error distributions.
Response errors are modelled by the Signal Discrimination Model (SDM): \[
y_t \sim \text{SDM}(c,\kappa).
\]
Deterministic arc-width update (algo4). On each trial the arc contracts toward 0 on a hit and expands toward \(\pi\) on a miss, with step-size \(\delta \in (0,1)\): \[
\tilde{a}_{t+1} = a_t\,(1-\delta) + \mathbf{1}\!\bigl[|y_t|>a_t\bigr]\,\delta\,\pi.
\]
Logit-noise stochastic extension. To make the model estimable, we add Gaussian noise on the unconstrained logit scale. Define \[
\tilde{x}_{t+1} = \operatorname{logit}\!\left(\tilde{a}_{t+1}/\pi\right),
\] then the stochastic transition is \[
x_{t+1} = \tilde{x}_{t+1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_\varepsilon^2),
\] so that \(a_{t+1} = \pi\,\sigma(x_{t+1})\) is guaranteed to lie in \((0,\pi)\) without clipping.
Joint log-likelihood. Because \(x_{t+1} \mid a_t, y_t\) is normal, the full log-likelihood decomposes as \[
\ell(\theta) =
\underbrace{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log f_{\text{SDM}}(y_t \mid c,\kappa)}_{\text{response errors}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\log\phi\!\left(x_{t+1};\; \tilde{x}_{t+1},\; \sigma_\varepsilon\right)}_{\text{arc transitions}},
\] with fitted parameter vector \(\theta=(c,\kappa,\delta,\sigma_\varepsilon)\). Below we verify identifiability via simulation-based parameter recovery and maximum-likelihood estimation with optim.

SDM component — the density of each response error \(y_t\)

title: Arc width and continuous reproduction
text:
In the standard continuous reproduction paradigm, participants study a visual feature (e.g., a color) and later reproduce it on a continuous scale (e.g., a color wheel). The angular error between the response and the target is taken as a measure of memory precision — but a single trial’s error is just a sample from a distribution, not a direct measure of that trial’s memory quality.
In the uncertainty estimation procedure, participants additionally draw a symmetric arc around their point response, indicating the range of plausible values consistent with their memory. Participants are incentivized to set the arc wisely: points are awarded as
\[
p = (\pi - \alpha) \cdot \mathbf{1}[|y| \le \alpha],
\]
where \(y\) is the signed response error and \(\alpha\) is the half-width of the arc. Wider arcs are safer (more likely to capture the target) but earn fewer points, creating an accuracy–confidence tradeoff.
This website documents analyses, simulations, and model-fitting results.

title: Model diagnostics: contraction-expansion (algo4) with logit noise, Bayesian
text:
Task and model summary
On each trial a participant reports a remembered color (continuous response) and sets a symmetric arc of half-width \(a_t \in (0,\pi)\) around it. Points are awarded as \[
p_t = (\pi - a_t)\,\mathbf{1}\!\bigl[|y_t| \le a_t\bigr],
\] where \(y_t\) is the signed response error. Wider arcs are safer but earn fewer points, creating an accuracy–confidence tradeoff. Empirically, participants’ arc widths are near-optimal given their error distributions.
Response errors are modelled by the Signal Discrimination Model (SDM): \[
y_t \sim \text{SDM}(c,\kappa).
\]
Deterministic arc-width update (algo4). On each trial the arc contracts toward 0 on a hit and expands toward \(\pi\) on a miss, with step-size \(\delta \in (0,1)\): \[
\tilde{a}_{t+1} = a_t\,(1-\delta) + \mathbf{1}\!\bigl[|y_t|>a_t\bigr]\,\delta\,\pi.
\]
Logit-noise stochastic extension. To make the model estimable, we add Gaussian noise on the unconstrained logit scale. Define \[
\tilde{x}_{t+1} = \operatorname{logit}\!\left(\tilde{a}_{t+1}/\pi\right),
\] then the stochastic transition is \[
x_{t+1} = \tilde{x}_{t+1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad
\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_\varepsilon^2),
\] so that \(a_{t+1} = \pi\,\sigma(x_{t+1})\) is guaranteed to lie in \((0,\pi)\) without clipping.
Joint log-likelihood. Because \(x_{t+1} \mid a_t, y_t\) is normal, the full log-likelihood decomposes as \[
\ell(\theta) =
\underbrace{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log f_{\text{SDM}}(y_t \mid c,\kappa)}_{\text{response errors}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\log\phi\!\left(x_{t+1};\; \tilde{x}_{t+1},\; \sigma_\varepsilon\right)}_{\text{arc transitions}},
\] with parameter vector \(\theta=(c,\kappa,\delta,\sigma_\varepsilon)\).

title: Model diagnostics: contraction-expansion (algo4) with logit noise, Bayesian
section: Custom brms family and Stan code
text:
Custom brms family and Stan code
We define a brms custom family whose log-likelihood is implemented by the sdm_algo4_lpdf Stan function in stan/sdm_algo4_likelihood.stan. The SDM numerator and normalization are provided by bmm’s Stan chunks.

sdm_algo4 <- custom_family(
  "sdm_algo4",
  dpars = c("mu", "c", "kappa", "delta", "asigma"),
  links = c("tan_half", "identity", "log", "logit", "log"),
  type = "real",
  loop = FALSE,
  vars = "vreal1"
)

stanvars <- sdm_base_stanvars() +
  stanvar(
    scode = read_file("stan/sdm_algo4_likelihood.stan"),
    block = "functions"
  )

title: Model diagnostics: contraction-expansion (algo4) with logit noise, Bayesian
text:
Priors
For c and kappa we use the default bmm priors. For delta and asigma we use a weakly informative prior that has more mass close to 0 but allows potentially larger values for normalization.

prior <- set_prior("constant(0)", dpar = "mu", class = "Intercept") +
  set_prior("student_t(5, 2, 0.75)", dpar = "c", class = "Intercept") +
  set_prior("student_t(5, 1.75, 0.75)", dpar = "kappa", class = "Intercept") +
  set_prior("normal(-3.5, 2)", dpar = "delta", class = "Intercept") +
  set_prior("normal(-3.5, 2)", dpar = "asigma", class = "Intercept")

Parameter recovery
Assess parameter recovery for the Bayesian version by simulating many datasets, fitting each with brms, and extracting only summary statistics and convergence diagnostics (not saving full fits).

n_recovery <- 1000  
n_trials <- 1000
set.seed(2026)

recovery_true <- tibble(
  iter = seq_len(n_recovery),
  c = runif(n_recovery, 1, 10),
  kappa = runif(n_recovery, 1, 10),
  delta = runif(n_recovery, 0.01, 0.5),
  sigma_e = runif(n_recovery, 0.01, 1)
)

fit_one_bayes <- function(iter, c, kappa, delta, sigma_e) {
  sim <- run_arc_algorithm(
    arc_update_fun = algo4_logit_noise(delta = delta, sigma_e = sigma_e),
    c = c, kappa = kappa, init_arc = pi / 2, n_trials = n_trials
  )
  sim_data <- tibble(y = sim$y, a = sim$a)
  
  fit <- tryCatch(
    brm(
      bf(y | vreal(a) ~ 1, c ~ 1, kappa ~ 1, delta ~ 1, asigma ~ 1),
      prior = prior,
      data = sim_data, family = sdm_algo4, stanvars = stanvars,
      backend = "cmdstanr", cores = 4,
      refresh = 0, silent = 2
    ),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (is.null(fit)) {
    return(tibble(
      iter = iter, c_est = NA, kappa_est = NA, delta_est = NA, sigma_e_est = NA,
      rhat_max = NA, neff_min = NA, converged = FALSE
    ))
  }
  est <- tryCatch({
    s <- fixef(fit)[-1, 1]
    list(
      c = exp(s["c_Intercept"]),
      kappa = exp(s["kappa_Intercept"]),
      delta = inv_logit(s["delta_Intercept"]),
      sigma_e = exp(s["asigma_Intercept"])
    )
  }, error = function(e) list(c = NA, kappa = NA, delta = NA, sigma_e = NA))
  rhat_max <- max(posterior::rhat(fit), na.rm = TRUE)
  tibble(
    iter = iter,
    c_est = est$c, kappa_est = est$kappa,
    delta_est = est$delta, sigma_e_est = est$sigma_e,
    rhat_max = rhat_max, converged = (rhat_max < 1.1)
  )
}

On each trial a participant reports a remembered color (continuous response) and sets a symmetric arc of half-width \(a_t \in (0,\pi)\) around it. Points are awarded as
\[
p_t = (\pi - a_t)\,\mathbf{1}\!\bigl[|y_t| \le a_t\bigr],
\]
where \(y_t\) is the signed response error. Wider arcs are safer but earn fewer points, creating an accuracy–confidence tradeoff. Empirically, participants’ arc widths are near-optimal given their error distributions.
Response errors are modelled by the Signal Discrimination Model (SDM):
\[
y_t \sim \text{SDM}(c,\kappa).
\]
Arc-width updates follow a noisy stochastic-gradient rule on the logit-reparameterized arc \(x_t = \operatorname{logit}(a_t/\pi)\). Define a soft hit indicator and gradient:
\[
s_t = \sigma\!\left(\frac{a_t - |y_t|}{\tau}\right), \qquad
g_t = -s_t + (\pi - a_t)\,\frac{s_t(1-s_t)}{\tau},
\]
with a decaying learning rate \(\delta_t = \delta_0/(t+1)^{0.5}\). The state transition is \[
x_{t+1} = x_t + \delta_t\bigl(g_t + \varepsilon_t\bigr), \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_g^2).
\]
Joint log-likelihood. The full log-likelihood decomposes as
\[
\ell(\theta) =
\underbrace{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log f_{\text{SDM}}(y_t \mid c,\kappa)}_{\text{response errors}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\log\phi\!\left(x_{t+1};\; x_t + \delta_t\, g_t,\; \delta_t\,\sigma_g\right)}_{\text{arc transitions}},
\]
with parameter vector \(\theta=(c,\kappa,\tau,\delta_0,\sigma_g)\). To ensure positivity, all parameters are estimated on the log scale.

section: Custom brms family and Stan code
text:
Custom brms family and Stan code
We define a brms custom family whose log-likelihood is implemented by the sdm_algo5_lpdf Stan function in stan/sdm_algo5_likelihood.stan. Use log links for all parameters except the fixed intercept mu (tan_half). Important: c is also on

sdm_algo5 <- custom_family(
  "sdm_algo5",
  dpars = c("mu", "c", "kappa", "tau", "delta", "sigmag"),
  links = c("tan_half", "identity", "log", "log", "log", "log"),
  type = "real",
  loop = FALSE,
  vars = "vreal1"
)

stanvars <- sdm_base_stanvars() +
  stanvar(
    scode = read_file("stan/sdm_algo5_likelihood.stan"),
    block = "functions"
  )

title: Model diagnostics: noisy-gradient (algo5), Bayesian
text:
Priors
We use weakly informative priors on the log scale for the algorithm parameters, centered roughly on plausible values (\(\tau \approx 0.025 \implies \log \approx -3.7\); \(\delta_0 \approx 0.1 \implies \log \approx -2.3\); \(\sigma_g \approx 2 \implies \log \approx 0.7\)). Also we must ensure initial values for tau and delta are small, otherwise the sampler gets confused.

prior <- set_prior("constant(0)", dpar = "mu", class = "Intercept") +
  set_prior("student_t(5, 2, 0.75)", dpar = "c", class = "Intercept") +
  set_prior("student_t(5, 1.75, 0.75)", dpar = "kappa", class = "Intercept") +
  set_prior("normal(-3.5, 2)", dpar = "tau", class = "Intercept") +
  set_prior("normal(-2.5, 2)", dpar = "delta", class = "Intercept") +
  set_prior("normal(0, 2)", dpar = "sigmag", class = "Intercept")

init_algo5_brm <- function() {
  tau_init <- log(runif(1, 1e-6, 0.05))
  delta_init <- log(runif(1, 1e-6, 0.5))
  list(
    Intercept_mu = 0,
    Intercept_c = runif(1, -2, 2),
    Intercept_kappa = runif(1, -2, 2),
    Intercept_tau = tau_init,
    Intercept_delta = delta_init,
    Intercept_sigmag = runif(1, -2, 2)
  )
}

text:
Parameter recovery
Assess parameter recovery for the Bayesian version by simulating many datasets, fitting each with brms. Spot check with just a 100 datasets (~ 17 minutes) - the MLE recovery diagnostics tested it for 10000 and showed great recovery. The likelihood is the same, so I expect similar performance, but the bayesian fits are slower. So this is a sanity check.

n_recovery <- 100
n_trials <- 1000
set.seed(2026)

recovery_true <- tibble(
  iter = seq_len(n_recovery),
  c = runif(n_recovery, 1, 10),
  kappa = runif(n_recovery, 1, 10),
  tau = runif(n_recovery, 0.001, 0.05),
  delta0 = runif(n_recovery, 0.01, 0.2),
  sigma_g = runif(n_recovery, 0, 10)
)

fit_one_bayes <- function(iter, c, kappa, tau, delta0, sigma_g) {
  sim <- run_arc_algorithm(
    arc_update_fun = algo5_noisy_grad(
      tau = tau, delta0 = delta0, delta_pow = 0.5, sigma_g = sigma_g
    ),
    c = c, kappa = kappa, init_arc = pi / 2, n_trials = n_trials
  )
  sim_data <- tibble(y = sim$y, a = sim$a)
  
  fit <- tryCatch(
    brm(
      bf(y | vreal(a) ~ 1, c ~ 1, kappa ~ 1, tau ~ 1, delta ~ 1, sigmag ~ 1),
      prior = prior,
      data = sim_data, family = sdm_algo5, stanvars = stanvars,
      backend = "cmdstanr", cores = 4, init = init_algo5_brm,
      refresh = 0, silent = 2
    ),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (is.null(fit)) {
    return(tibble(
      iter = iter, c_est = NA, kappa_est = NA, tau_est = NA,
      delta_est = NA, sigma_g_est = NA,
      rhat_max = NA, converged = FALSE
    ))
  }
  est <- tryCatch({
    s <- fixef(fit)[-1, 1]
    list(
      c = exp(s["c_Intercept"]),
      kappa = exp(s["kappa_Intercept"]),
      tau = exp(s["tau_Intercept"]),
      delta = exp(s["delta_Intercept"]),
      sigma_g = exp(s["sigmag_Intercept"])
    )
  }, error = function(e) list(c = NA, kappa = NA, tau = NA, delta = NA, sigma_g = NA))
  
  rhat_max <- max(posterior::rhat(fit), na.rm = TRUE)
  tibble(
    iter = iter,
    c_est = est$c, kappa_est = est$kappa,
    tau_est = est$tau, delta_est = est$delta, sigma_g_est = est$sigma_g,
    rhat_max = rhat_max, converged = (rhat_max < 1.1)
  )
}

recovery_est_bayes <- with_cache(
  "output/algo5_recovery_bayes.rds",
  purrr::pmap_dfr(recovery_true, fit_one_bayes)
)

title: Experiment Description & Data Codebook
text:
Experiment 1

Motivation
In the standard continuous reproduction paradigm, participants study a visual feature (e.g., a color) and later reproduce it on a continuous response scale (e.g., a color wheel). The angular error between the response and the target indexes memory precision — but a single trial’s error is just a sample from an underlying distribution, not a direct readout of that trial’s memory quality.
To obtain a trial-level uncertainty estimate, participants additionally drew a symmetric arc around their point response, indicating the range of values they consider plausible. An incentive-compatible scoring rule ensured that participants were motivated to set this arc thoughtfully.


Participants
Forty participants (four groups of 10) each completed two experimental sessions. The four groups differed in which experiment they performed in each session:

Set size & Set size
Set size & Time
Time & Set size
Time & Time.

Thus, some participants performed the same experiment twice, while others performed both experiments (see experimentorder and exp_cond below). Participants ranged in age from approximately 18–30 years.



Stimuli
On each trial, 1–8 colored circles appeared at evenly-spaced positions around a central fixation point. Colors were drawn from a 360° color wheel with a random offset on every trial (recorded in colorwheel0degree). Unused item slots were coded as 999 (= NA) in the raw data.


Procedure
Each trial proceeded as follows:

Encoding — The memory array appeared for a fixed duration (encodingtime; 0.1 s, 0.5 s, or 1.5 s depending on condition).
Retention interval — A blank delay followed (delay; 0.5 s, 1.0 s, 3.0 s, or 5.5 s depending on condition).
Point response — One item was cued (testposition). A color wheel appeared and the participant clicked to report the remembered color. The angular position of the response is recorded as responseangle.
Arc setting — The participant adjusted a symmetric arc centered on their point response, indicating the range of colors they believed could contain the target. The half-width of this arc (in degrees) is recorded as arcsize.





Scoring
Points on each trial were computed as:
\[
p = (\pi - \alpha) \cdot \mathbf{1}[|y| \le \alpha],
\]
where \(y\) is the signed response error (difference between the response and the correct color, in radians) and \(\alpha\) is the arc half-width (in radians). If the true color fell within the arc, the participant earned \(\pi - \alpha\) points; otherwise they earned 0. This creates an accuracy–confidence tradeoff: wider arcs are more likely to capture the target but yield fewer points.


Design
The experiment used two within-subject manipulations organized into separate session types:

Manipulation

In the set-size sessions, each block contained trials with all eight set sizes in random order (set size always 1 item in the time condition sessions). In the time sessions, encoding duration and retention interval were crossed factorially.

Full technical details

Participants
Forty students (26 female) from Sun Yat-sen University aged between 18 and 24 years (M=20) were recruited to participate in this study. They all had a normal or corrected-to-normal vision. The participants received 30 CNY per hour after completing the experiment. Participants gave written informed consent before their participation. The experimental protocol was approved by the institutional review board at the Department of Psychology, Sun Yat-sen University. There are two experiments, the Set size experiment, and the Time experiment. On two separate days (1-22 days between experiments, M=4), participants were randomly assigned to perform one of the two experiments. That is, there were four groups regarding different combinations of these two experiments. Each participant completed two Set size experiments / Set size then Time experiments / Time then Set size experiments / two Time experiments.


Stimuli and apparatus
The program of each experiment was prepared under MATLAB 2019a with PsychToolbox extensions and implemented on a Windows 10 (64-bit) desktop computer with a 27-inch LCD (60Hz of refresh rate) and a standard QWERTY keyboard in a dark laboratory room with acoustic shielding. The monitor was placed 57 cm away from the participant. Participants were shown colored dots (1.26° radius) of eccentricity 5.3° on a gray background (20 cd/m2), which occurred at one of the eight potential locations selected from an octagon. The color wheel was 1° thick and was centered on the monitor with a radius of 8°. It consisted of 360 equidistant colors from the CIE Lab space (centered at L = 54, a = 18, and b = 8; radius of 59). The sample colors were randomly selected with a minimum difference of 15 degrees from the color wheel. All colors had equal luminance (roughly 20 cd/m2).


Procedure

Set size experiment
A trial began with a 500-ms fixation (Figure 1). In the memory display, there were 1~8 colored dots. After a 1000-ms blank screen, participants reported the color of the item probed by a white circle on a color wheel, by clicking the left mouse button. A bar of the clicked color (length = 1°, thickness = 0.5°) would occur on the clicked location. Then they reported the uncertainty of their memory by adjusting the arc width centered on their first click (arc thickness = 0.5°, radius = 9°). If the true color was within their reported arc, participants got points inversely related to the arc size (points = 180 – arc width, where arc width is the size in degrees of one-half the symmetric arc). If the arc did not include the presented color, they got 0 points to discourage giving very small intervals. The total points and the points of the current trial would be presented on the screen until they pressed the space key. There was a 1000-ms interval between trials.
There was a 1-min break every 80 trials. There were 10 practice trials and 800 trials (10 blocks) in the formal experiment with 100 trials for each set size condition. Within each block, there was roughly an equal number of trials for each set size, and that the order of set sizes was randomized.


Time experiment
A trial began with a 500-ms fixation (Figure 2). In the memory display, there was always one colored dot, randomly occurring on one of the eight fixed locations. The colored dot was presented for 100ms/ 500ms/ 1500ms. Then there was a blank screen for 0.5s/ 3s/ 5.5s. Participants then reported the color of the item probed by a white circle on a color wheel, by clicking the left mouse button. Then they reported the uncertainty of their memory by adjusting the arc width centered on their first click. The points would be calculated and presented in the same way with Set size experiment. There was a 1000-ms interval between trials. There was a 1-min break every 81 trials. There were 10 practice trials and 810 trials (10 blocks) in the formal experiment with 100 trials for each time condition (9 conditions, encoding time:100ms/ 500ms/ 1500ms, delay duration: 0.5s/ 3s/ 5.5s). Within each block, there was roughly an equal number of trials for each condition, and that the order of conditions was randomized.

The analyses so far show that subject arc behavior is near optimal, if we assume perfect knowledge about the response error distribution. This doesn’t mean that subjects have such knowledge. It might be possible to learn from the feedback on each trial and to adjust the arc width in a way that reaches optimal behavior.

title: Explore reinforcement learning algorithms
section: Algorithm 4: Increase/decrease proportionally by arc remaining / arc used
text:
Algorithm 4: Increase/decrease proportionally by arc remaining / arc used
\[
a_{n+1} = \cases{
   a_n - \delta \, a_n = a_n \left(1 - \delta \right) & if hit, \\
   a_n + \delta \left(\pi-a_n\right) = a_n \left(1 - \delta \right) + \delta \pi & otherwise
}
\]

algo4(delta = 0.01) |> 
  run_arc_algorithm(n_trials = 1000) |> 
  plot_algorithm_run()








cs1 <- seq(0, 10, 0.1)
deltas <- c(0.001, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5)
pars <- expand.grid(c = cs1, delta = deltas)

out <- purrr::pmap(pars, \(c, delta) run_arc_algorithm(algo4(delta), c = c))
pars$phits <- sapply(out, \(x) x$phit)
pars$reward <- sapply(out, \(x) mean((pi - x$a)*(abs(x$y) <= x$a)))

sdm_optim <- lapply(cs1, \(c) find_optimum_sdm(c, kappa = 3))
sdm_optim <- do.call(rbind, sdm_optim)
sdm_optim$reward <- sdm_optim$phit * (pi - sdm_optim$alpha)

plot(cs1, sdm_optim$phit, type = "l", lty = "dashed", ylab = "Hit rate")
for (i in seq_along(deltas)) {
  lines(cs1, filter(pars, delta == deltas[i])$phit, col = i+1)
}
legend("topleft", legend = c("sdm optimal", deltas), col = seq_len(length(deltas)+1), lty = 1)







What this algorithm is doing is optimizing for the arc width a that satisfies:
\[
a = \pi (1 - F(a))
\]
where F is the cdf of the sdm.
This is similar to our objective but not exactly. That said, I decided to plot the achieved reward by the algorithm, rather than the hit rate, and compare it to the reward you get from the theoretical optimum:

plot(cs1, sdm_optim$reward, type = "l", lty = "dashed", ylab = "Mean reward")
for (i in seq_along(deltas)) {
  lines(cs1, filter(pars, delta == deltas[i])$reward, col = i+1)
}
legend("topleft", legend = c("sdm optimal", deltas), col = seq_len(length(deltas)+1), lty = 1)







Despite the mismatching hit rate, it gets really close to the optimum reward, and only starts diverging more as c increases. This suggests that the gradient of the reward function might be gentle enough so that near the optimum point it can accomodate trade-offs between the arc and the hit rate with a huge decrement in the reward achieved.
This will need more exploration but at least it seems like a plausible candidate (and/or with some modifications).
Here are more detailed individual runs:

  alg_list = list(algorithm4 = algo4(delta = 0.01)),
  c = c(0, 2, 4, 8, 16),
  n_trials = 800,
  n_runs = 10,
  init_arc = pi/2,
  plot_what = c("reward", "hit", "a"),
  add_oracle = TRUE,
  oracle_fun = \(c) find_optimum_sdm(c, kappa = 3),
  seed = 1
)

title: Explore reinforcement learning algorithms
section: Algorithm 5: Gradient ascent via smooth learner
text:
Algorithm 5: Gradient ascent via smooth learner
Smooth approximation to hits to allow for gradient climbing (with \(\tau\) being a tuning parameter):
\[
s = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\Bigl(-\frac{a-|y|}{\tau}\Bigr)}
\]
\(s = 0.5\) if your arc response was right at the boundary; \(s\) approaches 1 for hits further away from the boundary, and 0 for misses further away from the boundary.
Then you can get stochastic gradient ascent via the update rule:\[
a_{n+1} = a_n + \delta_i\Big[-s + (\pi-a)\frac{s(1-s)}{\tau}\Big]
\]

algo5(tau = 0.025, delta0 = 0.1, delta_pow = 0.5) |>
  run_arc_algorithm(n_trials = 1000, init_arc = pi/2) |>
  plot_algorithm_run()








taus <- c(0.01, 0.02, 0.05)
pars <- expand.grid(c = cs1, tau = taus)

out <- purrr::pmap(pars, \(c, tau) run_arc_algorithm(algo5(tau = tau, delta0 = 0.1, delta_pow = 0.5), c = c))
pars$phits <- sapply(out, \(x) x$phit)
pars$reward <- sapply(out, \(x) mean((pi - x$a)*(abs(x$y) <= x$a)))


plot(cs1, sdm_optim$phit, type = "l", lty = "dashed", ylab = "Hit rate")
for (i in seq_along(taus)) {
  lines(cs1, filter(pars, tau == taus[i])$phit, col = i+1)
}
legend("topleft", legend = c("sdm optimal", taus), col = seq_len(length(taus)+1), lty = 1)







More detailed individual runs:

spaghetti_single_runs(
  alg_list = list(algorithm5 = algo5(tau = 0.025, delta0 = 0.1)),
  c = c(0, 2, 4, 8, 16),
  n_trials = 800,
  n_runs = 10,
  init_arc = 1.0,
  plot_what = c("reward", "hit", "a"),
  add_oracle = TRUE,
  oracle_fun = \(c) find_optimum_sdm(c, kappa = 3),
  seed = 123
)







Visualizing algorithm 5
The abstract form of the algorithm equation makes it difficult to see how it works. So let’s visualize how the arc width will be updated depending on the distance between the arc and the response. Assume that the target is at a distance \(\pi/2\) from the response, and vary the arc half width around the response. If the arc is less than \(\pi/2\) then it’s a miss (right side); otherwise it’s a hit (left side)

update_fun <- algo5(tau = 0.025, delta0 = 0.1, delta_pow = 0.5)

old_a <- seq(0, pi, 0.01)
new_a <- sapply(old_a, \(a) update_fun(a = a, y = pi/2, i = 1))
plot(old_a, new_a, type = "l", xlab = "Old arc", ylab = "New arc")
abline(v = pi/2, lty = 2)
abline(0, 1, col = "red")







That was unexpected. It is an interesting algorithm, which we can summarize as:

if it’s a hit and the arc is much wider than the target, contract
if it’s a miss and the arc is much smaller than the target, do nothing
if the arc boundary is close to the target, regardless of whether it’s a miss or hit - expand.

The intuition is that if your arc is much smaller than the target, the fact that you miss can be due to chance - you know that even with a very precise memory some samples will be expected to deviate. When your arc is much bigger and you hit, you try to make it smaller. But if you are very close to the target, whether you hit or missed doesn’t matter - a small change would have pushed you over from a hit to a miss or vice versa, and we know that there is sampling noise. So you increase the arc to be safer, proportionally to how close the call was.
I didn’t design the algorithm this way, but it makes sense. For completeness, let’s look at the same figure, but also varying where the target is. Above I used a target that is a quarter of the circle away.

expand_grid(old_a = old_a, y = seq(0, pi, length.out = 9)) |>
  mutate(new_a = purrr::pmap_dbl(list(old_a, y), \(a, y) update_fun(a = a, y = y, i = 1)),
         y = round(y, 2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = old_a, y = new_a)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = factor(y))) +
  geom_abline(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = y), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Old A", y = "New A", color = "Target") +
  facet_wrap(~y)







Right, so it’s always the same principle, except that the amount of expansion when we are close to the target is biggest when the target was very close to the response, and smallest if it was on the opposite side of the circle. This makes sense - if the target is on the other side of the circle, and our arc is already big enough to be close to it, we don’t expand much. But if the target is close to the origin, and our arc is really small, then expand a lot because “we are in danger”. This fits the discussion we had about “the cost of errors” - when we have a small arc that is near optimal, changes to are a lot more costly, because an increment would lead to a lot more misses than the same increment if the optimal arc was much bigger.

Noise in execution with clipping
We let
\[
a_{t+1} = u(a_t, u_t, \theta_a) + \epsilon_t

where \(\epsilon_t\) is normally distributed noise, and we restrict to \([0, \pi)\).

title: Explore reinforcement learning algorithms
section: Noise in execution (added to unconstrained variable)
text:
Noise in execution (added to unconstrained variable)
To avoid the need to clip responses to be between 0 and pi, which will make estimation difficult, we can add the noise at a latent unconstrained version of the arc response. Since the arc varies from 0 to pi, we can use the logit function. Therefore:
\[
a_{t+1} = \sigma(\sigma^{-1}(u(a_t, u_t, \theta_a)/ \pi) + \epsilon_t)\pi
\]
where
\[
\sigma(x) = 1 / (1 + \exp(-x))
\]
and
\[
\sigma^{-1}(p) = \log(p/(1-p))
\]
For algorithm 4, everything is stable as before, so we could use this for stable estimation:

logit_noise <- function(..., sd, algo_fun) {
  inv_logit(logit(algo_fun(...)/pi) + rnorm(1, sd = sd))*pi
}

ribbon_summary_runs(
  alg_list = list(
    algo4 = algo4(delta = 0.1), 
    algo4_noise_0.1 = \(...) logit_noise(..., sd = 0.1, algo_fun = algo4(delta = 0.1)),
    algo4_noise_0.2 = \(...) logit_noise(..., sd = 0.2, algo_fun = algo4(delta = 0.1)),
    algo4_noise_0.3 = \(...) logit_noise(..., sd = 0.3, algo_fun = algo4(delta = 0.1))
  ),
  cs = c(8),
  n_trials = 1000,

  add_oracle = TRUE,
  oracle_fun = \(c) find_optimum_sdm(c, kappa = 3),
  seed = 1
) + ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Explore reinforcement learning algorithms
text:
Noise gradient
Alternatively, we can add noise directly to the gradient. To make this clearer, here’s a summary of the entire model.
Deterministic ingredients
Soft hit indicator
Introduce a smooth proxy for \(\mathbf 1\{|y_t|\le a_t\}\) with temperature \(\tau>0\): \[
z_t = \frac{a_t - |y_t|}{\tau},
\qquad
s_t = \sigma(z_t) = \frac{1}{1+\exp(-z_t)}.
\]
Gradient term
Define the gradient-like update term \[
g(a_t,y_t;\tau)
= -s_t + (\pi-a_t)\,\frac{s_t(1-s_t)}{\tau}.
\]
Learning-rate schedule
Use a decaying step size \[
\delta_t = \frac{\delta_0}{(t+1)^{\delta_{\text{pow}}}},
\qquad \delta_0>0,\ \delta_{\text{pow}}>0.
\]
Noisy-gradient dynamics
A direct stochastic version of the update adds Gaussian noise to the gradient term. Because \(a_t\) must remain in \((0,\pi)\), it is convenient to work on an unconstrained scale.
Reparameterization
Let \[
x_t = \operatorname{logit}\!\left(\frac{a_t}{\pi}\right)\in\mathbb R,
\qquad
a_t = \pi\,\sigma(x_t).
\]
State transition
The stochastic transition is \[
x_{t+1}
=
x_t + \delta_t\Big(g(a_t,y_t;\tau) + \varepsilon_t\Big),
\qquad
\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal N(0,\sigma_g^2),
\] with \(a_t=\pi\sigma(x_t)\).
Equivalently, conditioning on \((x_t,y_t)\), \[
x_{t+1}\mid x_t,y_t,\theta
\sim
\mathcal N\!\left(
x_t+\delta_t g(\pi\sigma(x_t),y_t;\tau),
\ (\delta_t\sigma_g)^2
\right),
\] where the parameter vector is \[
\theta = (\tau,\delta_0,\delta_{\text{pow}},\sigma_g).
\]
Likelihood for fitting \((a,y)\)

Arc component:
The likelihood for the arc component is: \[
p(a_{2:T}\mid a_1,y_{1:T-1},\theta)
=
\prod_{t=1}^{T-1}
\mathcal N\!\left(
x_{t+1}\ \Big|\ x_t+\delta_t g(a_t,y_t;\tau),\ \delta_t\sigma_g
\right),
\]
where \[
x_t = \operatorname{logit}(a_t/\pi),\quad a_t=\pi\sigma(x_t).
\]
Joint component (log likelihood)
If I also want to model the distribution of \(y_t\) (with \(\kappa\) fixed or estimated), then
Taking logs: \[
\log p(y_{1:T},a_{2:T}\mid a_1,\theta)
=
\sum_{t=1}^T \log f_{\mathrm{SDM}}(y_t\mid 0, c, \kappa)
+
\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}
\log \phi\!\left(
x_{t+1};
x_t+\delta_t g(a_t,y_t;\tau),
\ \delta_t\sigma_g
\right).
\]
with \(\phi\) being the log density of the normal distribution.
Summary of fitted parameters
A minimal, well-posed parameterization is: \[
\theta = (c, \kappa, \tau,\delta_0,\delta_{\text{pow}},\sigma_g),
\]
Simulation
The algo5_noisy_grad function in R/arc-models.R implements this model. Unlike the logit-noise wrapper (which computes the deterministic update on the native scale and then perturbs on the logit scale), here the entire update—gradient plus noise—is applied on the unconstrained logit scale \(x_t = \operatorname{logit}(a_t/\pi)\).

ribbon_summary_runs(
  alg_list = list(
    algo5_det = algo5_noisy_grad(tau = 0.025, delta0 = 0.1, sigma_g = 0),
    noisy_grad_0.5 = algo5_noisy_grad(tau = 0.025, delta0 = 0.1, sigma_g = 0.5),
    noisy_grad_1 = algo5_noisy_grad(tau = 0.025, delta0 = 0.1, sigma_g = 1),
    noisy_grad_2 = algo5_noisy_grad(tau = 0.025, delta0 = 0.1, sigma_g = 2),

Because the noise multiplies \(\delta_t\) (which decays over trials), even substantial \(\sigma_g\) values do not destroy convergence — the effective noise variance \((\delta_t \sigma_g)^2\) shrinks automatically with the learning rate. Compare this with the logit-noise execution variant, where fixed noise continually perturbs the arc and prevents convergence for algorithm 5.
